title: States of Matter: Gases and Liquids
tagline: Intermolecular forces, gas laws, ideal gas equation, kinetic theory and molecular speeds, deviation from ideal behaviour, van der Waals equation, liquefaction, vapour pressure, viscosity and surface tension.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ISC Class XI Chemistry syllabus. States of Matter is part of the established ISC Class XI Chemistry scope, but its exact inclusion in the latest revised policy is unverified; this chapter follows the established syllabus scope and is labelled accordingly. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Matter can exist in different states because the balance between thermal energy and intermolecular forces is different in each state. In a gas, the particles move almost independently; in a liquid, they are close but can still move past one another. This chapter looks at the gas laws and the ideal gas equation, then at the kinetic model of gases and the idea of molecular speeds. It also explains why real gases do not always behave ideally, introduces the van der Waals equation, and finishes with the properties of liquids such as vapour pressure, viscosity and surface tension, which are understood in terms of intermolecular forces.

learn.title: Characteristics of the states of matter

blocks.text: The three common states differ mainly in how strongly the particles interact and how much freedom they have to move. Solids have definite shape and volume because particles stay in fixed positions. Liquids have definite volume but take the shape of the container. Gases have neither definite shape nor definite volume and expand to fill the container. The differences are ultimately due to the relative strengths of intermolecular forces and thermal motion.

items: Solids have definite shape and volume.
Liquids have definite volume but not definite shape.
Gases have no definite shape or volume.
The differences come from thermal motion and intermolecular forces.

items.text: Water in a glass is liquid and takes the shape of part of the glass, while steam expands to fill the whole container as a gas.
items.note: The same substance can appear very different in different states because the balance of forces changes.

blocks.text: The gas laws describe how pressure, volume, temperature and amount of gas are related for an ideal gas. Boyle's law says that at constant temperature, volume is inversely proportional to pressure. Charles's law says that at constant pressure, volume is proportional to absolute temperature. Gay-Lussac's law says that at constant volume, pressure is proportional to absolute temperature. Avogadro's law says that equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.

items: Boyle's law: V is proportional to 1/P at constant T.
Charles's law: V is proportional to T at constant P.
Gay-Lussac's law: P is proportional to T at constant V.
Avogadro's law: V is proportional to n at constant T and P.
Use kelvin temperature in all gas-law calculations.

items.text: If a gas is compressed to half its volume at constant temperature, its pressure doubles, in agreement with Boyle's law.
items.note: The temperature must be kept constant for Boyle's law to apply directly.

blocks.text: The ideal gas equation combines the gas laws into a single relation: PV = nRT. It describes an ideal gas, one in which the particles are treated as having negligible volume and no intermolecular attraction. The equation is very useful because many gases come close to this behaviour at low pressure and high temperature. The value of R depends on the units chosen for pressure, volume and temperature.

items: PV = nRT is the ideal gas equation.
It assumes negligible molecular volume and no intermolecular forces.
Real gases approximate it at low pressure and high temperature.
R has different numerical values for different units.

items.text: For one mole of an ideal gas at 300 K and 1 bar, V = RT/P, and the result is about 25 litres if the units are chosen consistently.
items.note: This calculation shows why units matter: using the wrong R or the wrong pressure units gives a wrong volume.

blocks.text: The kinetic theory treats a gas as a large number of point particles in constant random motion, colliding with each other and with the walls of the container. The pressure comes from these collisions. From this model, the temperature of a gas is linked to the average kinetic energy of its molecules. There is also a range of molecular speeds: some are slow, some fast, and the most probable, average and root-mean-square speeds are different ways of describing that range.

items: The kinetic model assumes point particles in random motion.
Pressure comes from molecular collisions with the walls.
Temperature is related to average kinetic energy.
Molecules have a distribution of speeds.
There are most probable, average and root-mean-square speeds.

items.text: At the same temperature, lighter gas molecules move faster on average than heavier ones, because the average kinetic energy depends on temperature, not directly on mass.
items.note: This is one reason hydrogen leaks more readily and diffuses faster than heavier gases.

blocks.text: Real gases do not always obey PV = nRT, especially when the pressure is high or the temperature is low. The ideal gas model ignores the finite size of molecules and the attractions between them. When these become important, the real gas is less compressible than an ideal gas would be, or it condenses into a liquid. The deviation can be seen by comparing PV/nRT with the ideal value of 1.

items: Real gases deviate from ideal behaviour at high pressure and low temperature.
Ideal behaviour assumes no molecular size and no attraction.
Deviation is larger when molecules are near each other.
Liquefaction shows that real gases are not ideal.

items.text: At very high pressure, the volume of the molecules themselves becomes important, so the gas is harder to compress than the ideal equation would predict.
items.note: The deviation is a sign that the simple assumptions of the model are breaking down.

blocks.text: The van der Waals equation is a simple improvement on the ideal gas equation. It corrects for the finite volume of the molecules by subtracting a term from the volume, and it corrects for intermolecular attraction by adding a term to the pressure. The constants a and b are different for different gases. The equation is most useful when explaining why real gases deviate from ideality and when a gas is near condensation.

items: The equation corrects for molecular volume and attraction.
The constant a relates to intermolecular attraction.
The constant b relates to molecular volume.
It reduces to PV = nRT when the corrections are small.

items.text: A gas with a larger a value usually has stronger intermolecular attractions, so it is more easily liquefied.
items.note: The van der Waals constants give a simple way to compare how different gases behave.

blocks.text: A gas can be liquefied by applying pressure and lowering the temperature, but only if the temperature is below a certain value called the critical temperature. Above the critical temperature, a gas cannot be liquefied by pressure alone, because the thermal motion overcomes the attractions. The critical temperature is one way to compare how easy it is to liquefy different gases.

items: Liquefaction requires low temperature and high pressure.
Above the critical temperature, a gas cannot be liquefied by pressure alone.
Critical temperature is a characteristic of each gas.
Lower critical temperature usually means weaker intermolecular attractions.

items.text: A gas with a high critical temperature is easier to liquefy than one with a low critical temperature, because its molecules attract each other more strongly.
items.note: Critical temperature is a practical way of comparing gases, not just a theoretical idea.

learn.title: Liquid state: vapour pressure, viscosity and surface tension

blocks.text: In a liquid, molecules are close together and experience significant intermolecular attractions. These forces give the liquid its important properties. Vapour pressure is the pressure of vapour in equilibrium with the liquid at a given temperature. Viscosity is a measure of a liquid's resistance to flow, and strong intermolecular forces usually make a liquid more viscous. Surface tension is the tendency of the liquid surface to contract, and it also depends on attractive forces between molecules.

items: Vapour pressure is the equilibrium pressure of vapour above a liquid.
Viscosity measures resistance to flow.
Surface tension makes the liquid surface behave like a stretched membrane.
All three depend on intermolecular forces.

items.text: Honey is more viscous than water because the attractive forces between its molecules are stronger, so it flows more slowly.
items.note: Viscosity is not the same as density; a thick liquid is not necessarily heavy, just slow to flow.

keyPoints: Solids, liquids and gases differ in shape, volume and freedom of motion.
Gas laws describe ideal gas behaviour and must use kelvin temperature.
PV = nRT is the ideal gas equation.
Kinetic theory links pressure and temperature to molecular motion.
Real gases deviate from ideal behaviour at high pressure and low temperature.
The van der Waals equation corrects the ideal gas equation for molecular volume and attraction.
Vapour pressure, viscosity and surface tension depend on intermolecular forces.
examFocus: When using gas laws, always convert temperature to kelvin; using Celsius where kelvin is required is a common source of error.
When explaining deviations from ideal behaviour, mention both molecular size and intermolecular attraction, not just one of them.

vocabulary.meaning: A gas that obeys PV = nRT exactly, with negligible molecular volume and no intermolecular attraction.
The law that volume is inversely proportional to pressure at constant temperature.
The law that volume is proportional to absolute temperature at constant pressure.
A model that explains gas behaviour in terms of moving molecules.
The pressure of vapour in equilibrium with a liquid at a given temperature.
The property that makes the surface of a liquid contract like a stretched membrane.

questions.prompt: Boyle's law applies when the following are constant:
questions.explanation: Boyle's law is for a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting that temperature must be constant for Boyle's law.

questions.explanation: The ideal gas equation is PV = nRT.
questions.commonMistake: Misplacing R or mixing units so the equation no longer balances.

questions.prompt: State one reason real gases deviate from ideal behaviour.
questions.answer: Real gases have molecules with finite volume and intermolecular attractions, which the ideal gas model ignores.
questions.explanation: These two factors make real gases less ideal at high pressure and low temperature.
questions.commonMistake: Saying only that real gases are impure, or giving an answer that does not mention molecular size or attraction.

questions.prompt: Why does a liquid have a definite volume but not a definite shape?
questions.answer: Because the molecules are close enough to stay together, but not fixed in place, so they can flow to take the shape of the container.
questions.explanation: This is the typical behaviour of a liquid, intermediate between a solid and a gas.
questions.commonMistake: Saying a liquid has no volume, or that it keeps a fixed shape like a solid.

questions.prompt: Explain why hydrogen molecules move faster on average than oxygen molecules at the same temperature.
questions.answer: At the same temperature, the average kinetic energy of the molecules is the same. Since kinetic energy is 1/2 mv^2, lighter molecules must have a higher average speed. Hydrogen is much lighter than oxygen, so its molecules move faster on average.
questions.explanation: This follows from temperature being linked to average kinetic energy, not from the mass being directly proportional to speed.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking faster molecules must have more kinetic energy, or forgetting that mass matters.
